summary: Redwood ran a targeted Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations for Suncrest AI. Discussion covered how to model cost/latency tradeoffs in the Console, how prefix and KV cache reduce token counts, batching windows and latency SLOs, and a proposed POC with dedicated capacity. topics: Prefix cache vs KV cache tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46m
Attendees: Jared Klein (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Ava Chen (Suncrest CTO), Ravi Malhotra (Suncrest ML Eng), Sara Velez (Suncrest PM)

[00:00] Jared: All right, thanks everyone for joining. Quick intro — i'm Jared, AE on the infra team, and Maya is our SE who will run through the Optimize playbook for batching and caching. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Ava: Good, thanks. We want to focus on lowering per-token cost without blowing our latency SLOs. We have a 300ms P95 target for chat flows.
[00:15] Maya: Perfect, that's helpful. Quick agenda — we'll show the Console Optimize tab, run a couple of cost sims (hosted vs dedicated), and then dig into prefix cache and the KV cache behaviors. We'll call out batching windows, prefetching strategies, and the expected delta in tokens.
[00:28] Ravi: Sounds good. We have some long chat contexts — like 4–6k tokens sometimes — and multi-turn with shared prefixes.
[00:35] Lena: Cool. I'll share my screen — jumping into the Console. Okay, Console > Optimize > Workloads. Here's the cost-sim wizard. (murmur) bear with me, it's a little slow on my laptop.
[00:48] [00:48] Maya: First, baseline — hosted API, gpt-ish open model we recommend, average request size 450 tokens, average response 120 tokens, traffic 40 reqs/s. Our sample cost estimate — roughly $X/1M tokens on this model — but we'll plug in exact numbers in the workbook.
[01:05] Ava: Wait — can you show how the tokens are counted when prefix cache applies? That's the part we're trying to understand.
[01:10] Maya: Yes. Two parts: prefix cache eliminates re-sending the shared prompt prefix tokens to the model by using a cached KV snapshot; KV cache stores keys/values for Transformer attention. When we can reuse an existing prefix, the system issues a short call with only the new user tokens and points the runtime at the cached KV state. So tokens billed drops to only the deltas often — in many of our customers we see 30–70% token reduction depending on prefix reuse.
[01:33] Ravi: So it's not just prompt length, it's the number of new tokens you send plus the cached state retrieval, right?
[01:38] Maya: Exactly. The runtime does a small metadata lookup to find the KV handle; that is not billed as tokens. We still count output tokens for generation. There are edge cases with recompute where we have to rehydrate and that will add to cost, but Optimize highlights those.
[01:52] [01:52] Jared: Important to call out — prefix cache tends to be most effective for multi-turn chat with a stable system prompt and many similar conversation openings. If your product has highly unique each time prompts, you'll get less win.
[02:03] Sara: Our product also does a lot of rerank steps — multiple short calls that hit a shared context. Does the cache help there too?
[02:09] Maya: Yes, rerank and candidate scoring often get big wins. Because those calls reuse the same context and differ only in the candidate, KV/prefix reuse can cut tokens dramatically.
[02:18] [02:18] Lena: switching to batching — in the Console we expose suggested batching windows: micro-batch 10–25ms, medium 50–100ms, or adaptive. Here's a sim: at 40 reqs/s, a 25ms window increases throughput by ~1.6x but adds median latency of ~8–12ms. For the P95 you care about, we recommend measuring P95 drift in your traces if you buy higher batch windows.
[02:42] Ravi: Our 300ms P95 is tight. If batching adds variability, we'd rather keep latency and pay cost.
[02:49] Maya: Totally fair. In the cost-sim workbook we prepared three scenarios — conservative (no batching), balanced (25ms window on non-interactive endpoints), and aggressive (50ms across inference with prefix caching). I'll send the workbook.
[03:02] [03:02] Ava: Can you show a real example where switching a prompt to prefix cached reduces tokens in the Console?
[03:07] Lena: Sure — example time. Here's a customer conversation with a system prompt of ~600 tokens and a 5-turn exchange. With prefix cache on, Console shows 'tokens saved: 2.1k' and cost delta — that's about 48% reduction for that session in hosted pricing. Without cache, you pay for the whole 600 + turns each time. See the trace linked here: /console/trace/abc123 (note: placeholder).
[03:31] [03:31] Maya: A caveat: prefix cache uses a namespace and key: if you change the system prompt, you need a new prefix key. For A/B prompts you can shard keys by prompt-hash. Also TTL management — we default to 24 hours in hosted but you can tune TTLs for application semantics.
[03:51] Sara: Does prefix cache affect model drift or evaluation — like when we A/B prompts?
[03:55] Maya: The model output only depends on the state and the new tokens supplied; if you change system prompt and forget to invalidate the prefix, results will be wrong. So we recommend prompt-hash tracked in your app and explicit invalidation on prompt edits. We'll share examples in the docs.
[04:12] [04:12] Ravi: Tell me more about KV cache eviction and memory — for dedicated pools are we going to blow GPU memory with lots of cached prefixes?
[04:18] Maya: Good question. On dedicated pools we control per-GPU KV capacity and eviction policy. The runtime stores KV shards and we have hot sets pinned; less-used prefixes are spilled to cheaper storage or evicted. In practice, we size the KV store by expected concurrent sessions with large contexts. The Console has a KV heatmap in Observability to show evictions and hit-rate.
[04:36] [04:36] Lena: Also note, the memory cost is independent of tokens billed — it's infra overhead. In Dedicated pricing we surface the expected GPU footprint.
[04:45] [04:45] Jared: Let's talk about batching heuristics — two knobs: max batching window and request grouping by seq length. Grouping similar-length requests increases packing efficiency and reduces wasted compute.
[04:58] Ravi: Do you do dynamic batching based on arrival rate?
[05:01] Maya: Yes, adaptive batching combines short windows at low qps and increases window slightly when throughput is high to hit utilization targets. But it's always bounded by your latency SLOs.
[05:11] [05:11] Ava: How do we model cost for prefetching? We sometimes want to prefetch likely next-turn completions for speed, but that doubles generation.
[05:18] Maya: Prefetching is a deliberate trade: you pay for tokens generated speculatively. In the workbook we show a metric named "speculative token overhead" — percent of generated tokens that were not subsequently used. If your UI makes prefetchings and 60% of those never get used, it's wasted. The Optimize tab lets you run sims with prefetch rate and spec-overhead assumptions.
[05:37] [05:37] Sara: Any examples of customers who used prefetch smartly?
[05:40] Maya: One customer prefetched only for users with high click-probability (derived from a model) and combined that with short TTL prefix cache; net cost was up 8% but perceived latency dropped 150ms for 80% of sessions — so they accepted the budget increase.
[05:57] [05:57] Jared: Security quick check — Ava asked earlier about data residency and logs. Our hosted runs allow configurable retention (30/90/365d) for logs and audit trails; for regulated data we'd recommend Private (VPC or on-prem). SSO/SAML and RBAC are available for Dedicated and Private.
[06:14] Ava: For the pilot, we probably need SSO and 90-day retention. Is that supported on a Dedicated pilot?
[06:19] Jared: Yes. Dedicated pilot can come with managed SSO and 90-day retention in the control plane, or for stricter rules we can deploy Private. We'll scope that in the POC doc.
[06:28] [06:28] Ravi: Back to numbers — can you walk the math of batch window impact? Say we 40 reqs/s and 25ms window — how many requests per batch and what's the latency shift?
[06:36] Maya: At 40 reqs/s you get on average 1 request every 25ms, so 25ms window typically batches 1–2 requests — increases GPU packing by ~30–60% depending on length distribution. Median latency adds the window time but the GPU step gets amortized. In the workbook we modeled average payload length and used empirical kernel efficiency curves; I'll share the file.
[06:58] [07:00] Lena: I'm toggling to the Optimize > Simulations tab. Here's scenario A: No caching, no batching. Cost: baseline $Y/month for X tokens. Scenario B: prefix cache on with TTL 24h and 25ms batching on scoring endpoints — saves ~27% monthly. Scenario C: prefix+KV caching + 50ms batching + prefetch 20% — saves 42% but P95 increased ~40ms.
[07:24] Ava: That P95 delta might be acceptable if it's 40ms, still under 300ms. But we need to see tail behavior under spikes.
[07:31] Maya: Agreed. We'll recommend running stress tests with your traffic trace. That's why we asked for a 7-day trace.
[07:37] [07:37] Ravi: On instrumentation — does Console give token-level cost by route? We need to break down feature-level unit economics.
[07:43] Lena: Yep — Console has per-route dashboards, token counts, cost, and ability to tag routes. You can filter by model, region, and cache-hit-rate. We can export CSVs and tie them to your invoice.
[07:54] Sara: There's also the question of model variants — quantized 4-bit models vs FP16. Any guidance?
[07:59] Maya: In Optimize we recommend a mix: use quantized for high-throughput low-latency inference when output quality is acceptable. The cost sim includes per-token cost differences for quantized vs full models and includes fallback rules — e.g., if quality drift exceeds threshold we route to higher precision.
[08:14] [08:14] Jared: Quick interruption — customer asked about multi-region failover. If we route to another region, prefix handles must be region-aware or globally replicated, and that affects cache-hit rate. We'll note that in the POC doc.
[08:28] Ava: Good point. We'll likely run primary in us-east and failover in eu-west.
[08:32] Maya: For cross-region failover we recommend short TTLs and warming the prefix cache proactively after failover.
[08:38] [08:38] Lena: jumping to a short live demo — i'm going to flip a toggle that changes batch window from 0 to 25ms on a staging route. You'll see the live trace — median latency ticks up slightly, batching increases pack efficiency (you can see the GPU utilization chart). OK toggled. Give it a sec.
[08:55] [09:00] (brief pause, system noises)
[09:03] Ravi: I see some noise in the trace — median now 26ms higher but P95 only up 12ms. That's fine.
[09:11] Maya: Exactly the kind of tradeoff.
[09:13] [09:13] Jared: We're about 9 minutes in; want to open up for Qs and then recap next steps.
[09:18] Ava: Quick one — for reranking we do 10 candidates per query. Would you recommend batching across candidates or do them sequentially?
[09:24] Maya: If candidates are independent calls, batching across them packs better but you risk cross-request latency coupling. Often we batch synchronous candidates only when the endpoint is tolerant of slight additional latency; otherwise use a scoring micro-batch with 10ms windows and specialized reranker kernels. We'll include reranker tuning notes.
[09:42] Sara: Any gotchas if we use both prefix cache and prefetch?
[09:46] Maya: Prefetch can invalidate some cache assumptions if you precompute variants; be mindful of duplicated KV entries for each speculative branch. Prefetch combined with careful TTLs and deduplication is the sweet spot.
[09:58] [09:58] (some laughter)
[10:00] Ava: Okay what's the proposed POC scope? You mentioned a dedicated pilot.
[10:05] Jared: Proposal: a 4-week pilot, dedicated pool sized for your peak concurrency (~50 concurrent gen sessions), enable prefix/KV cache, run two experiments: baseline vs optimized, capture P95 and total tokens for a 7-day synthetic trace. We include SSO and 90d retention. We'll provide the cost sim up front and an expected delta.
[10:23] Ravi: What about support SLA during pilot?
[10:26] Jared: 24/7 on-call for infra incidents and a weekly sync with a Solutions Eng.
[10:31] [10:31] Lena: And we'll instrument a 1-hour perf run before and after turning on cache+batches so you can see the direct delta. Maya will own the run.
[10:39] Maya: I'll coordinate with Ravi on the trace format — JSONL with timestamp, prompt hash, user id anonymized. Please remove PII.
[10:47] [10:47] Sara: One last security question: where are KV blobs stored? Are they encrypted at rest?
[10:53] Maya: Yes — KV blobs in hosted are encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys available for Dedicated/Private. Transit encryption is TLS. We also log access in audit events; retention is configurable.
[11:05] [11:05] Jared: Great. Quick recap and action items.
[11:09] Jared: Action items are in the notes — Jared to share spreadsheet, Maya to run perf with the trace once provided, Ava to confirm SSO. We'll aim to have the POC kickoff week of 2025-06-16.
[11:20] Ava: Sounds good, appreciate the walkthrough.
[11:24] Ravi: Thanks, lots to chew on.
[11:27] Lena: Thanks everyone — i'll drop the Console screenshots and the trace links in the follow-up.
[11:32] Jared: Bye all.

Notes on transcription: Several technical terms mis-transcribed in spots (e.g., "KV cahce" -> should be KV cache) and some speaker labels consolidated. The Console trace link above is a placeholder; we will attach real trace exports in follow-up.
closing_notes: Demo focused on concrete cost/latency tradeoffs; proposal for 4-week dedicated pilot. Follow-up: cost workbook, perf runs, and POC scheduling. Recommend Suncrest submit anonymized trace ASAP.
